title: Entertainment permits, legacy-business status and community grants
question: Are entertainment permits, legacy-business status and small community grants approved, limited or refused differently from one district or kind of area to another?
finding: The Entertainment Commission’s minutes (July 2022 to December 2025) record 287 permit items: none denied, 14 approved with limits added at the hearing and 35 put off or moved; by district the share not approved outright runs from 0.0% (District 10, 24) to 23.6% (District 9, 55). Of 135 legacy-business applications before the Small Business Commission (August 2022 to February 2026), 113 print a passing vote and none a denial, and the grant lists (325 Arts Commission grants, 89 Community Challenge Grants) show only winners, so refusals cannot be compared by area.
how: One row per permit item in the Entertainment Commission minutes, sorted by the words of the outcome line: approved with staff recommendations (the standard form); approved with an amendment, hours or another limit added at the hearing; continued or moved to the regular agenda; denied. Addresses are placed with the City’s address file, in the district lines in force on the date, and in 2020 census tracts ranked by 2020-24 Census measures. Legacy-business rows count applications in Small Business Commission minutes, which print no address and for some batches no outcome line, and the Historic Preservation Commission’s recommendations, which do. Grant rows count awards in the Arts Commission’s cultural-equity dataset (rows dated 2015 and 2016) and the City Administrator’s Community Challenge Grant lists. Groups under 20 are left out.
limits: Refusals at these bodies are close to invisible in the public record: an entertainment application may be withdrawn or held back before a hearing without the minutes showing it, and no body publishes unfunded grant applicants, so approval rates cannot be compared between areas for grants at all. Permit items are concentrated in a few districts and neighborhoods (the table shows which), so counts by tract follow where venues are, not who lives nearby. Limits added at a hearing are conditions of approval. Grant recipients’ addresses are not in these lists. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
